The Denver (Colorado)
The Denver (Colorado) Republican gives an account of the alleged bandit, H. M. Burton, who has been operating in that State. It will be remembered that Burton is supposed to have been one of the men who robbed the stage running between Alma and Fayetteville, in this State. The Republican says that Burton is now in the Denver jail charged with robbing the stage running between Del Norte and Alamosa, about midnight on the night of June 29. The robbery was one of the most audacious in the annuals of highway robbery, and links the name of the perpetrator with that of Billy LeRoy. The story of the deed is best told in the words of J. B. McMillan, one of the victims of the robbery. He said in substance:

"There were eight men and one woman inside the coach, and four men besides the driver on top. I was among the latter, sitting beside the driver. It was about midnight, I should think, and about twenty miles from Del Norte, when we were halted. It was very dark, and we were just turning a bend in the road when the word came to halt. There was only one man visible, to the left and about ten feet ahead of the coach. The robber was standing behind a piece of canvass stretched alongside the road, and had a revolver pointed directly at myself and the driver. He told us calmly to deliver ourselves and he would not harm us, but if we made a bad break he would shoot. I was on the side next to the robber, and I immediately got down from my seat followed by the driver. After we got down, the robber came from behind the canvas and placed over our heads a cloth cap, which came down to our shoulders and completely blinded us. He then ordered us to stand still, and himself went to the stage door and ordered the occupants to come out, one at a time, and take their positions in line alongside the driver and myself.

"He told the passengers not to make any unnecessary movements, as they were all covered by the guns of his men in concealment, and their lives were in jeopardy. After the passengers were all in line, he put caps similar to mine over their faces, tied their hands behind their backs, and then proceeded to rifle their pockets. He took nothing but money. Everything else he would replace just where he got it from. I do not know how much money he got. From me he got about $140, which he took from my pocketbook, replacing the pocketbook after taking the money out. He had a light burning in front of the canvass, behind which was a reflector, which shed the rays directly in our faces. He occupied about fifteen minutes in the search. He then ordered us to kneel, a row, and he proceeded to rifle the mail-bags. The woman, at his bidding, held the light for him while he did this. He opened only two sacks, I believe. He opened only us kneeling about half an hour. He kept talking all the time, using good language. In fact, during the whole time of the robbery he was very gentlemanly.

"He had a soft, mellow voice. He was not nervous or quick, but did the work in a business-like manner. He was a man nearly six feet in height, smooth face, had a heavy light mustache, and would weigh perhaps 165 pounds. He had on a dark hat and coat, and was not disguised in any way. After he had robbed the mail he skipped off into the darkness. When we found he had left we removed our caps, untied each other's hands, picked up the remnants of the mail, picked the mail bags and proceeded on to Alamosa. It is my opinion now that he did the work alone, and that his comrades being in the woods wns all a hoax.

Billy LeRoy robbed stages till sevenen months ago, when the United States Marshals chanced upon him at Denver, whither he had gone to visit a woman with whom he had fallen in love. Five policemen, two marshals and a secret service officer officer entered the house with drawn revolvers, and the bold knight of the road was taken into custody. He was tried before Judge Hallet last winter, convicted of robbing the mails, and sentenced to a long term of imprisonment in the government prison at Detroit. He received his sentence coolly, danced a jig in the prisoners' dock, and jocosely remarked that at the expiration of his sentence there would be no more stages to rob.

Something like two months ago, Deputy Marshal Sim Cantril left Denver with LeRoy en route for Detroit. They went by the way of the Kansas Pacific railway, and on the train was LeRoy's sweet heart and one of the members of his band, who had purchased tickets to Kansas City, and were traveling together as man and wife. During the night, when the marshal was in the toilet room and all in the car were sleeping, the colleague and sweet heart took off LeRoy's handcuffs, hastily dressed him in a suit of woman's clothes and he took the seat lately occupied by the woman, she going to another quarter of the car. Then the colleague raised the hue and cry that the prisoner had escaped. The train was nearing Hays City, Kansas, and at that point she descended from the car, while LeRoy and his man went on to Kansas City.

LeRoy was next heard from near Del Norte, robbing stages, and his capture and lynching quickly followed. The woman he so madly loved reisdes in Del Norte, and probably it was his infatuation for her that caused him to haunt that vicinity, and which led to his shocking death. During Billy LeRoy's border life he committed no less than eight known murders, and these atrocious deeds may form the basis of another letter.

The capture was effected on the Sabbath day, shortly before the sun was lost to sight behind the snowy peaks of the Great Second Range. LeRoy was painfully wounded in the left leg, and on reaching the rude jail in Del Norte, had almost bled to death. A physician was summoned, the wound dressed, and at 10 o'clock Billy was as "game" as though on the road with a band at his back. He made no confession, as was at first reported, but offered to wager the sheriff a basket of Mumm that he would be out of the "quay," as he termed the jail, and through Saquache Pass, before the U. S. Marshall could arrive from Denver. His brother, on the contrary, seemed to be in depressed spirits. Five special deputy sheriffs were sworn in and appointed guards to the bandit king, and were locked up in the jail—ranged around his cell in order to guard against any possibility of escape. The sheriff retired, and a few hours past midnight a scene occurred that was not down in the bills.

The first rumors of LeRoy's capture had spread through the camp like wildfire, and the miners quickly concluded that they would put one desperado out of the way before the mountain robbers could come to the rescue. A meeting was called in the principal saloon, and before midnight "Judge Lynch" had ordered the death of Billy LeRoy. The vigilantes numbered over one hundred of the best citizens and miners in the region of Del Norte. They went down to the jail in a body, overpowered the guards and going to LeRoy's cell the leader said:
"Billy, you're sent for."
LeRoy was lying on one elbow in his cell, and, with his customary bravado, replied:
"Really, I feel quite proud of this ovation, but, owing to the lateness of the hour, etc., I must decline."
The door was quickly unlocked, and the captive, realizing that a climax equally as lawless as his life was at hand, said:
"Don't be in a hurry, gentlemen, for the more flaste the less speed, and too many cooks spoil the broth."
He stood up while the already prepared noose was thrown over his head, and looking down at the coil of sea grass remarked that it was not finer than silk.
While the robber chief walked out of his cell with the blood gushing afresh from his wounded limb, his brother was so overcome by the situation that he was as helpless as an infant, and members of the vigilance committee were obliged to carry him forth.

"You make me blush," said Billy, in a scornful manner, looking at his brother; "you have been called, so why can't you quit like a man?"

A wagon stood in the jail yard and placing the doomed men upon it, the vigilantes dragged the wagon down to a clump of trees which stand by the river. A half dozen lanterns were in the crowd, and by the light LeRoy could see that several of the self-constituted executioners carried revolvers ready drawn.

"Put up your guns!" he cried, in his ringing voice; "I shant harm a hair on your heads."

The wagon came to a halt under a large projecting limb, and it was but the work of a minute to throw the loose end of each rope over the limb and knot it securely. Then the leader asked in solemn tones:

"Have either of you men anything to say?"

Billy looked at his brother who was too weak to speak, and then, as if courting a pistol shot, answered:

"Talk is cheaper than town lots in Aspen. Some men are known by the deeds that live after them, and I am one of that number. A brand-new baby in North Carolina rejoices in the devoted supervision of three great-grandfathers and two great-grandmothers.

On the night of Friday the 12th instant a most atrocious murder was committed about two miles from Abbeville in our Parish. On that night Pine Henderson a worthy colored man of our Parish was attending church in the town and one William Epperson also. Henderson had left his wife and daughter aged about fourteen at home, Epperson more or less under the influence of liquor, it is said, left church long before Henderson, uttering the most vilest imprecations against the whole people, white and black. After church, Henderson returns home, his bed and floor covered with blood, his wife murdered in a most fiendish manner and his daughter upon whom he doted with more than ordinary parental affection missing. The neighbors are notified, the officers of the law likewise. To them the horrid and ghastly sight presents itself of the mother litterally butchered, having received with an axe a first blow that split the cranium and produced instantaneous death ; but not satisfied with this the hellish monster, in human form, had severed the neck from the body, but a small particle of flesh and skin, keeping the two together, chopped off one of the hands, cut the throat from ear to ear and with one last stroke cut open her abdomen exposing the entrails of the aged victim. To the Editor of The Chicago Tribune.

DAVENPORT, Ia., Sept. 14.—"From the quiet level of the deep all hights and depths are measured," said a most eminent citizen a little more than a year ago, and now the lips which uttered those memorable words are trembling with the whisperings of months of pain and sickness. And there are those who remember that the originator of those words has said many things not only worthy of passing notice, but also which offer food for almost an illimitable amount of thought. From the years of life in that lowly log cabin in the Ohio forest, and no doubt from the influences fostered in the young mind by that noble mother, has sprung a mind whose works shall go down in history as worthy of a place beside those of Washington and Lincoln; and how similar to the latter has been the life of James A. Garfield.

The widow Garfield had prayed that bright things might come through her "Jinnle," and had often talked with him about the noble life she wished him to lead, but it seemed almost hopeless when the boy left the little home for a life on the canal; but still the little mother hoped and prayed for her boy. James came near losing his life one night in the canal; he fell overboard, but as luck, or may be it was Providence, would have it, the rope which he held in his hand kinked and caught on the gunwale of the boat, thus saving the life which is now so important a one to all of us. While the boy was in the water he thought in a few seconds of a great deal of his past life, and when he climbed all dripping to the deck something prompted him to try and make the rope kink over the gunwale again; but we will let him tell what followed:

"I have thrown this rope six hundred times; I might have thrown it ten times six hundred without its catching; ten times six hundred are six thousand; so there were six thousand chances against my life. Against such odds Providence alone could have saved it. Providence, therefore, thinks it worth saving; and if that's so I won't throw it away on a canal-boat. I'll go home and got an education, and become a man."

We all know that our country has been better off for the salvation of that life; if in nothing else, it shows the chances which lay before the poorest and most lowly.

How well he made a man of himself he has shown in a thousand ways. It is needless to pass over the years of toll and struggle in obtaining his education, we have all heard of them; but after all the regular courses were passed, and only what schooling the world in the years of his future life could give him lay before him, he wrote one day:

"Again the path
Leads o'er the summit where the sunbeams fall,
And thus in light and shade, sunshine and gloom,
Sorrow and joy, this pathway leads along."

And twenty years after he fell on the "summit" midst the "sunbeams," pierced by the bullet of a wretch. In the midst of his success, at the highest pinnacle which a human being can reach in this world, he fell, and the hearts of fifty millions of people fell with him. No man over stood more in the universal love of the people, and when we look back along his pathway we see the reasons.

NEGRO LABORERS.
NEW YORK, Aug. 5.—The announcement that a large number of negroes are on their way from the South to work on the New York, Ontario & Western Railroad has created great excitement among the men now employed by the contractors in the different sections. Thus far none have been engaged for Section No. 1, which commences at the west end of the new tunnel at Guttenberg and extends twenty-five miles, but on the Middletown branch, which embraces five sections, a distance of twenty-five miles, over 300 negroes are employed. They are employed in the gravel banks and rock cuts of the highlands and work at the low rate of $1.25 a day. One contractor, who holds a sub-contract from Douglass for building five miles of the Middletown section, has refused to employ any negroes, and has engaged only Irish and Italians. Another contractor on Section No. 1 announces his determination to bring on the colored men at all hazards, justifying his action on the ground that he can obtain a uniform rate of $1.25 a day, and that he can obtain 1,000 or more negroes, whereas the white laborers refuse to work at such a low rate.

THE NEGROES NOW EMPLOYED came mostly from Maryland and the District of Columbia, from which district another contingent is expected to arrive next week. The reports in regard to the number expected seems to have been so exaggerated that a meeting of the white laborers has been called for next Sunday, at Middletown, to protest against further importations. If a leaf ear be turned to their protest by the contractors a strike will certainly result, and serious trouble is expected. The contractors do not seem to be deterred by these threats, however, and what the end will be it is difficult to foresee.

The excitement among the white laborers of the New-York, Ontario and Western Railroad over the proposed action of the contractors to substitute colored men at $1 25 a day in the places of the Irishmen and Italians now employed at $1 60 a day, continues, and the feeling of the men has become intense. It is expected that the action taken at the meeting at Middletown to-day will determine the course of the men in case the threatened invasion of negroes takes place.

Many of the men are in favor of sending a petition to Mr. Tilden, who is a large stockholder in the road, asking him to interest himself in their cause. THE LABORERS AT MIDDLETOWN. The condition of the laborers, on the New-Yo
The condition of the laborers on the New-York, Ontario and Western Railroad, is now much quieter than was anticipated from the reports which reached this city from Middletown, of intended violence in case negroes from the South were put to work in the places of the Irish and Italians now employed. Donglass and Graves, the contractors of the Middletown division, say that they are now working five or six hundred men, nearly all Italians, and will today have two hundred and fifty more. They will procure white labor if they can, but if they cannot, an effort will be made to get negroes, who, they say, can do more work than the Italians. No white men will be discharged to make room for the negroes. The colored laborers at Cornwall receive $1.25 a day in gravel, and $1.50 a day in rock work. COLORED RAILROAD HANDS. MEN OF VARIOUS RACES PEACEFULLY WORKING IN ORANGE COUNTY.
Colored Men from the South brought on to Supply an Unfilled Demand on a Branch of the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad.

MIDDLETOWN, N. Y., Aug. 7.—Further investigation to-day of the rumors that a strike was intended by laborers near here on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad, because negro laborers in large numbers have been brought from the South, and more are coming, proves beyond a doubt that not only is there no strike, but also that none is anticipated. The reason why no disturbance is looked for is that the contractors are engaging all the workmen they can get in this vicinity, and also have agents in New York city who hire men and send them to work on the railroad between this city and the Hudson River. Even after these efforts to get help, the contractors lament that they no not have laborers enough. This raking and scraping the whole country round about us for day laborers has resulted in bringing together several races. In fact, Orange County was never so cosmopolitan as this summer.

The work on the projected railroads is in such a condition that the different races are brought closer together than they will probably be when the roadbed is graded. They do not, however, come into actual daily and social contact, but they live each in their own neighborhoods. The two large railroad enterprises to connect New York city with the West, by way of Buffalo and Lake Ontario, were begun in June last, and the most active operations are being carried on in this vicinity. One is the New York, Lake Shore and Buffalo Railroad, and the other the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad. The former is to run from Weehawken nearly to Albany, and then across the State to Buffalo. The New York, Ontario and Western is to run from Jersey City to Ontario, N. Y., and the two roads approach within twenty-five miles of each other at this point. They are to be connected by a branch railroad from Cornwall to this city, and it is on this branch that it was rumored that the strike was threatened.

The contractors for this 25-mile branch are Messrs. W. A. Douglas and Graves, and their headquarters are at Cornwall. Both Mr. Douglas and Mr. Graves said to your correspondent to-day that there was nothing but harmony among the workmen. Mr. Graves went on to explain that nearly 600 Italians are at work on the Cornwall end of the branch, while less than a hundred laborers, mostly Irishmen and residents of this section, were at work on the western end of the road. The section of five miles next to this city, Mr. Graves continued, was sublet last week to Contractors Evans and Ackerman of Binghamton. Mr. D'Arcy has been the contractor up to the present time, and the change of contractors may have aroused the fears of some of the Middletown laborers that the whole work is hereafter to be done by negro labor brought from the South. "The fact is," said Mr. Graves, "I asked Messrs. Evans and Ackerman what workmen they were to employ, and they said positively that Italians were to be brought to work. They are now using Italian labor in Binghamton.

"The negroes are at work on another part of the work from the Italians, Irish, and Yankees," continued the contractor. "They are blasting in the solid rock on the river front at Cornwall, on the projected main line from Weehawken. Good workmen they are, too. They are quicker in accomplishing work than white men, and far superior to the Italians. I account for it by their singing at their work. They work under Contractors McLaughlin and Riley, and they receive the same wages that the white men do. In removing earth they get $1.25 a day, but when they handle rock they get $1.50 a day. Very shrewd they are, too. When they are digging earth sometimes the grading has to be done through deep cuts. All about this hilly country the earth is full of stones as big as your hat, or much larger.

"Well, Pomp." I will sometimes say to one, 'how does it go?' He will straighten himself up and say, with a twinkle in his eyes:

"Well 'nuf, boss, on'y a dolla' 'n a qua'tah ain't 'nuf for dis yer kin' o' wuk. Luk o dat dar rock now,' kicking one over with his foot. 'doan you tink we's a wukin' in rock wuk; a dolla' 'n a 'af ain't none too much for rockwuk."

"You see, down South the negroes don't know anything about stones. Rocks is the term by which all kinds and sizes of stones go. About 160 negroes were first brought here from Washington and Baltimore in June. About half of these have deserted and gone to work on farms hereabouts. After work they go about in groups and sing Southern plantation songs and pick up coppers. No; I do not know that they have any camp meeting services or preaching on Sunday or any of the other characteristic goings on of their race. They like to lie out in the sun and sleep when off duty or on Sundays."

The Italians live in shanties along the line of the branch railroad and in two or three frame houses on the main line north of Cornwall, while the negroes live in houses in Cornwall and work south of that place. The Italians are supplied with rye bread by Louis Canterbury, who has a bakery looking out on the Hudson River. Louis is the Italian who transported a large force of Italians to Cape Cod not long ago to dig a canal, and was forced to bring them back to New York at a loss. Yesterday Louis said that he lost $5,000 by the operation, as he had to pay the men their wages. The banks of the river were made picturesque yesterday by half a dozen Italian women with their skirts tucked about them, red handkerchiefs on their heads, and standing with the water half way up to their brown knees, while they pounded and scrubbed their consorts' linen on the rocks.

COLORED LABORERS.
EXCITEMENT OVER THEIR EMPLOYMENT AS RAILROAD LABORERS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

New York, Aug. 11.—The excitement in regard to the employment of cheap colored labor by the contractors on the New York, Ontario & Western Railroad has not only not abated, but work has been actually suspended on some sections of the line north of Cornwall. Supplies which were ordered from this city for the use of the workmen have been countermanded. On the sections south of Cornwall the colored men are progressing steadily with their work at the fixed rate of $1.25 per day. The contractors show no disposition to yield to the

PROTESTS OF THE WHITE LABORERS, and the Directors of the railroad company have refused to interfere on the ground that the contractors are bound in heavy securities for the completion of their work and are not responsible to the Company for the means they may employ in constructing the road, provided the work be properly done. The action of the white laborers has had the effect of preventing the importation of colored men to the sections between Guttonberg and the terminus of the fifth section, but on the Middletown Branch, embracing five sections, a distance of twenty-five miles, the negroes are still retained.

LONGVIEW, October 17—We are permitted to condense the following from a special report sent to the Longview Democrat: The most horrible crime ever committed in this part of Texas was perpetrated last Wednesday, near Breckville, by a family of negroes named White. A family named Sloan had recently moved into the neighborhood to pick cotton on the farm of a Mr. Hill. A dispute between the Sloans, and a negro, Lum White, because of an accusation made by Lum that the Sloon children had been grabbing peanuts from the hills of Lum's patch. Lum went to the house of Sloan on Tuesday, and wanted to whip the children, but was prevented by Mrs. Sloan and her daughter, about fifteen years of age. For this he swore revenge, and next morning upon the plea that he would show her where some fine muscadines were the wife of Lum enticed the girl to a deep ravine, a secluded spot, where Lum was in waiting. While his wife held the girl Lum outraged her, and then using his pocket-knife, cut her bowels open both lengthways and crosswise, deliberately cutting off pieces of the entrails as they protuded, and scattered the fragments far and near. He then cut the girl's throat from ear to ear and left her body. When found at the inquest the woman confessed to all of the revolting details, when a young man named Hart, incesed at this cool recital of fendish brutality, shot the negro dead. The wife of Lum and an old negro who lived with them were started on their way to Carthage, but a crowd of men met the escort and took the prisoners and shot them.

HALTER AND PISTOL.
HIS DISHONOR JUDGE LYNCH'S WORK
Enacted by a Texan Mob Who Were Determined to Put an End to Wild Lawlessness.
HOUSTON, TEXAS, August 23.—The most intense excitement prevails at Orange, this State, over an attempt to assassinate Sheriff George Michael, and the subsequent lynching of eight of the leaders of the plot, who met death at the hands of citizens banded together for the purpose of putting an effectual stop to outrages and all kinds of lawlessness which have been openly committed in the neighborhood for the past few weeks.

The trouble began some three weeks ago, when O. L. Delno, a noted criminal, attempting escape, was shot by Detective Wood. When Delno's friends searched for Wood he could not be found. They then charged Sheriff Michael with concealing him, and vowed vengeance. Yesterday a diabolical plot to assassinate Michel was artfully arranged between Charles Delno and Dug Harris (white), and Samuel and Bob Saxon (colored). A sham saloon fight for the purpose of involving Michael was started by Sam Saxon, who started and ran toward the place where Charles Delno, Dug Harris, Bob Saxon, and a number of negroes were laying in ambush. When the Sheriff and posse reached the ambush they were fired upon. The former receiving buckshot wounds in all parts of his body.

One hundred and fifty citizens at once got together, thoroughly armed, and started in pursuit of the outlaws, who after the assault on the sheriff succeeded in making their escape. Four of the negroes were captured and immediately shot. Another negro, Robert Garcon, was tortured for an hour by being alternately hanged and resuscitated until he revealed the plot described above. After this confession, together with that of the other crimes, had been wrested from him, he was strung up for good and left hanging. Delno was captured and placed in jail, where Sam Saxon, though badly wounded, shortly after joined him. By eight o'clock at night the military guard, thinking everything secure, left the jail and repaired to their homes.

At nine o'clock a large body of exasperated citizens gathered at the jail, demanded of Deputy Sheriff Jett the release of Sam Saxon and his leading negro accomplice. This was refused, but the crowd overpowered him and dragged them out. A wild and thrilling scene then commenced. The negroes fell on their knees and throwing their arms around Deputy Sheriff Jett's legs implored him for God's sake to save them. Suddenly they were inspired with an idea of making their own escape and amid frantic yells started to run. The gathered crowd at once opened fire on them, riddling both bodies with buckshot and killing them instantly. The bodies were left where they fell, and the crowd dispersed. Charles Delno was not disturbed, but is to be tried to-day before a kangaroo court, Judge Lynch presiding. No sympathy whatever is expressed for those shot and hanged.
A reign of terror prevails. All business is suspended. Governor Roberts has been solicited to send troops to Orange, but refuses until it becomes apparent that the civil authorities cannot cope with the difficulties.

TROUBLE IN TEXAS.
A SERIES OF TRAGIC EVENTS.
The Sequences of a Scoundrel's Revenge—Ambushes, Murders and Lynchings—Attempt to Burn the Town of Orange—Quiet Not Yet Restored.
St. Louis, August 23.—Houston, Texas, specials report bloody tragedies which occurred at Orange during the past week, causing intense excitement along the Texas and New Orleans Railroad, and fears are entertained that something worse will follow. The present condition of affairs grew out of a difficulty which occurred three weeks ago between O. L. Delano, a noted desperado, and Detective Wood, in which Delano was seriously shot. Wood escaped, and Charles Delano, a brother of O. L. Delano, accused Sheriff Geo. Michael of aiding in the escape, and avowed that he soon would get even with him. With this view he concocted a plan to assassinate Michael, and was aided by Doug. Harris and two negroes, Sam and Bob Saxon.

The plan failed, but they succeeded in seriously wounding the Sheriff by leading him into an ambush. The citizens became greatly incensed at these proceedings, and one hundred of them congregated, captured four of the negroes and shot them. Bob Saxon was also captured, and after extorting a confession from him, in which he reviewed the plot to kill the Sheriff, he was hanged to a tree. Another negro was arrested and hanged, and Chas. Delano was captured and placed in jail. A hundred armed men scoured the neighboring swamps for others of the gang. A guard was placed around the jail the night before last to guard Delano. Sam Saxon, one of the leaders of the desperadoes, who was wounded, came into Orange yesterday and surrendered to the guard at the jail. At 8 o'clock last night the guard was disbanded and went home. An hour later a large body of men surrounded the jail, and the deputy sheriff being unable to hold it surrendered, and Sam Saxon and another negro of the gang were taken out and their bodies riddled with buckshot.

Before dying Saxon made a confession detailing some of the operations, one of which was an attempt to burn the town of Orange.

THE TROUBLE AT ORANGE.
Two More of the Negro Roughs Killed-Citizens Determined to Wipe out the Lawless Element.
Special Telegram to the N. O. Times.

News has just reached here to the effect that the trouble at Orange, Texas, has broken out afresh, and resulted in the killing of two more of the negro desperadoes who were in the gang which made the attack on Sheriff Michael a few days ago. Yesterday evening Bob Saxon, a notorious negro, and the one who shot down Michael, was arrested near Orange and brought to town, and placed in jail. Last night about twelve o'clock a band of citizens broke open the jail and taking Saxon and another negro out, shot them to death, their bodies being fairly riddled with bullets. At present two white desperadoes, Charlie Delno and Dug Harris, are confined in the jail charged with instigating the lawless element of the town to assassinate the sheriff. The feeling against Delno and Harris is very bitter and it is probable they will be lynched before the trouble is over. For quite awhile the law abiding people of Orange have quietly borne the outrages perpetrated by the roughs of the town, but they now realize that forbearance is no longer a virtue, and are determined to shoot every cut throat they can lay their hands upon. Not more than six weeks ago the roughs had things so much their own way that at night they would fire at brakemen on freight trains, and shoot out the headlights of the locomotives and otherwise amuse themselves. From what can be learned seven of these characters have been killed by the enraged citizens, and it is likely that many more of them will share the fate. The citizens say they will not cease until they have cleared the town of the gang of desperate men who have done so much to injure the good name of Orange.

KANGAROO JUSTICE.
Up here we call it Lynch law, but down in Texas the term is too mild and they give it the more vigorous name of Kangaroo law. A conspicuous case of its administration occurred on Sunday at a little town named Orange, on the Texas and New Orleans railroad. For months past the place had been dominated by a gang of desperadoes. One of the most noted among them was O. L. Delno, whom a detective named Wood had shot in an attempt to arrest, and against whom the vengeance of the gang was at once directed. But sheriff Michel had helped Wood to get away, and now a plot was laid to shoot the sheriff. A noted negro ruffian named Sam Saxon was to raise a row, so as to have the sheriff pursue him, when the negro was to lead him to a spot where half a dozen of the gang lay in ambush. The plot succeeded, and as the sheriff in pursuit passed the ambuscade he was fired upon and probably mortally wounded. This so enraged the decent people of the town that they armed themselves to a man resolved to destroy the desperadoes. They scoured the woods, with the deputy sheriff at their head, and the same day caught four of the desperadoes and shot them, one of them, after being tortured, confessing that Delno was the author of the plot to shoot the sheriff. Next Delno was captured and placed in jail, with several other members of the gang, a strong guard being placed around the jail. In the night, however, finding all quiet, the guard dispersed, and soon afterwards about 20 armed men surrounded the jail and compelled the jailor to open the door. They took out Sam Saxon and another negro and shot them, deciding to try Delno next day by a Kangaroo court. Delno, however, who has several brothers also connected with the gang, is connected by marriage with some of the best families in the neighborhood, who had enough influence to have him released on bail. As, however, quite a number of the gang are still at large, it is believed when his trial comes off there will be more trouble. The gang have been the terror of the neighborhood for years, giving the town a bad name and paralyzing it, business, and the determination is that the whole band of outlaws shall be cleaned out.

Sheriff Michael Shot.
Orange was brown into intense excitement Wednesday night by the shooting of George W. Michael, our brave and gallant sheriff; and the killing and hanging which followed as a natural result of the rage and indignation of the community. To give minute details of the affair is impossible at this writing, but below we present a brief and as accurate a statement as possible.

Shortly after dark, Sam. Saxon, colored, and two or three other negroes made an assault upon a white man, Gus Garvey, in the Sample Room Saloon, several shots being fired. It seems that Saxon had threatened to shoot Garvey early in the evening and that the latter had purchased a shot gun to defend himself, but from some cause did not use his gun successfully. No one was hurt by the shooting. Sheriff Michael and deputy Ferguson were close by and started immediately in pursuit of the negroes, being joined by three or four others. When the posse reached a point just beyond Mr. A. Gilmer's residence and near negro town, they ran suddenly upon the negroes, who, it appears, were lying in ambush, and in an instant the posse was fired into, a shotgun charge taking effect in Mr. Michael's right arm and side. The posse fired, shooting Sam Saxon and another negro down, the others escaping. It was then discovered that the sheriff was dangerously hurt; news to the effect reached town, and in five or ten minutes at least one hundred and fifty citizens were in arms and in pursuit of the negroes. They were excited, and believing at the time that the sheriff was mortally wounded, left no stone unturned to capture the whole gang. Their success manifested itself the next morning in the shape of Robert Saxon, a brother of Sam's, hanging to the large oak in front of D. Call & Son's store, two others killed and a number wounded. We should state just here that Sam Saxon, after the shooting at the saloon, ran with his crowd out towards negro town, where he was joined by a num-
some discoveries the next morning caused a suspicion that the whole affair was a deep laid plan to kill the sheriff and deputy, and warrants were issued for the arrest of several white men as the originators, one of them being Charlie Delano, who was promptly arrested and placed in jail. Several negroes were also arrested, as accessories, and jailed. sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-21.A17:
The Rioting in Orange.
[Special Correspondence to the Galveston News, Aug. 22.]
The rioting in Orange still continues and the wildest excitement prevails. About 8 o'clock last night the Orange Rifles, considering everything quiet and there being no visible signs of any intended outbreak, disbanded and returned to their homes, leaving the jail unguarded. About one hour later an armed party of citizens surrounded the jail and demanded its surrender. Deputy Sheriff Rance Jett, who was in charge, seeing that it was useless to contend with the overpowering force yielded up the jail. The invaders at once entered and took out Sam Saxon, the ringleader of the negro desperados, and another negro, said to be an accomplice. Saxon is the negro who escaped after the affray last week, but was so closely pursued by his hunters that he came up on Sunday morning and gave himself up and was placed in the jail for safe-keeping. Upon being taken out of the jail by the mob, Saxon's courage failed him, and he dropped on his knees at the deputy sheriff's feet, and throwing his armis around Sheriff Jett's legs, implored God's mercy upon his soul. Recognizing that all hope was gone, and that they were to be killed, Saxon and the other negro became frantic in their efforts to escape, and their terrifying yells of "murder" could be heard at a great distance. The exasperated citizens endeavored to quiet them, but to no avail, and at once filled their bodies full of buckshot. A general stampede was made by the congregations of the various churches, which were at worship, and the ministers fled their churches without a benediction.

Some startling confessions were made by Saxon before his death. He testified that he had been paid by Charles Delano to steal a carload of cattle last fall from the Louisiana Western Railroad, and that a certain woman connected with the desperadoes had offered him $500 to burn the town, that the spoils of a plot to which she was a party, might be reaped by herself and confederates. He attempted to accomplish this end but failed, only succeeding in burning one house and store, last fall.

A trial of Charles Delano was to have taken place at 9 o'clock this morning, at which Judge Lynch was to preside, and it is probable that by this time his neck will have been broken. Many of his accomplices are still at large, including his four brothers-in-law, the Harrises, and Ol. Delano and two negroes, but they are being trailed down and will, in all probability, be captured and suffer the penalty inflicted by an enraged community.

The latest news from Orange is that Delano, on being admitted to bail, secured his bondsmen against loss, and left Orange county, with several of his male relatives, apparently forever. Everything is quiet at Orange now.
sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-21.A19:
Terror's Reign in Texas Dispatch to the Globe-Democrat
HOUSTON, Texas, August 25.—A meeting of 300 of the leading colored people of Galveston yesterday, and which called attention to the bloody outrages perpetrated on negroes at Orange by an armed mob of white citizens, and denouncing Governor Roberts and the state government for declining to interfere, has aroused a still higher degree of public interest in the late wholesale lynching in this state. The Galveston News is the leading paper in Texas, and several days ago called upon the state government to interfere and stop this dreadful slaughter of human beings, who were utterly helpless in the hands of a mob; but Governor Roberts has remained utterly silent. The facts of the whole business are that for six years a feud has existed between two parties at Orange, one composed of citizens of the town and its young white men, and the other of male members of two or three leading families in the surrounding country—the Harrises and others. Chas. Delano, the alleged leader of the opposition party, is a white man of 35, and married into the Harris family. He is a stock raiser and cattle man, and his followers, called by the citizens of Orange his gang, include, besides his kinsmen, some eight or ten negroes, two of them named Robert and Sam Saxon, mulates, and reputed sons of one of the prominent white citizens of the vicinity. As stated in the dispatch, Bob Saxon was hung in Wednesday's riot of last week, and his brother Sam was shot dead by a mob last Sunday night. Latterly Charles Delano was regarded as the leader of the Saxon, or negro, party, and Sheriff Michael of that of the citizens, and for months past a difficulty was expected. All sorts of crimes have been laid to the charge of the Saxon party, among them the robbery of the express agent at Orange by two masked men, and a short time ago the theft of cattle. Of course the citizens' party only waited for a chance at their opponents, and got it, but in the riot last week, when Sheriff Michael was shot, it has not been established, as stated by Michael's party, that the Saxon party were the first to fire on him, or that there was an ambush of negroes waiting to assassinate the sheriff, as claimed. Mrs. Delano, whom Sam Saxon

charged with hiring him for $500 to burn the town, is a lady with spirit and influence enough with her relatives to stir up a movement for revenge in case her husband is hung, as has been threatened by the lynchers. It is not believed that the friends of the Saxons will let the matter rest, but the reign of terror now existing in Orange may change into a reign of assassination. Persons who saw the shooting of the two negro prisoners taken from the Orange jail on Sunday night, say it was most horrible and brutally. The cries of the poor wretches were pitiful as they clung to the knees of the officers for protection, in the face of a mob of thirty men, but they were shot down like dogs. Orange is now completely at the mercy of the mob, who hung one negro and shot four others to death without a semblance of a trial. Delano's friends assert he had nothing to do with inciting the negroes to fire at Sheriff Michael.

ODD SHIPMENTS BY EXPRESS.

Babies, Bears Snakes, and Other Queer Articles of Freight.

"Odd freight? Well, I should say we have," said R. F. Masters, one of the oldest clerks in the main office of the Adams express company, on Market street, as he twirled himself around on his high stool and faced an inquiring reporter yesterday afternoon. Mr. Masters talks with great volubility, and, as he has a habit of dropping many small words, his conversation was decidedly jerky. "Yes, we ship a little of everything, from diamonds to Chester white pigs and Limberg cheese. Remarkable thing about that cheese. Ever smell any? Rich, penetrating sort of fragrance, ain't it? Case burst in freight room last spring. Made every one sick. Two Irishmen tried to shovel it up. Smell nearly turned 'em inside out. Got a Dutchman, regular out-and-out eat-a-sandwich-in-a-minute sort of a fellow, from Bergmyer's saloon across the way, but he gave out in ten minutes. Only finished it with a box of deodorizer. Phew! They should charge double rates to ship such stuff," and the speaker elevated his nose as though a trace of the diabolical aroma still lingered in his nostrils.

"Two babies have come through this office, one from Chicago for New York and the other from Washington to this city. The men on this line made a great fuss when the Chicago young one was shipped. Telegraph operators all along the route sent dispatches ahead and crowds of people went to the depots to see the baby. Came all the way in the express cars. Had a hammock rigged up. New idea, you know, and messengers thought it was a kind of a joke, but they wouldn't like too much work of that kind. Baby's mother died in Chicago, father lived in New York; weighed forty-one pounds, I believe; cost about two dollars and a half to send it through. Philadelphia baby came along some time after. Both made their trip first-class, and seemed to enjoy things generally. Fed 'em on regular spoon victuals from hotels along the line. Ofted have dead folks shipped. Don't know why they should send them by express tho', 'Tain't likely ane one's going to walk off with a corpse. Yes, a man shipped three Short-horn cattle clean through to Nebraska about a month ago. Unless he got 'em for nothing, they must have cost him a power of money when he got them. Just think of a man expressing a whole deer carcass two or three thousand miles. About as sensible for a butcher to express a beef through from here to Camden. Last fall a lunatic sent a twelve hundred pound block of cedar from California to New York. That's nothing, however, for I see some one sent twenty barrels of mess pork to the Pottstown military camp by express, and the charges amounted to over $100. A cinnamon bear came through from Nevada by express last January for the Zoological Garden. Said he was tame when they shipped him. Got loose near Omaha, drove every one out of car, chewed up half a deer, ripened among the freight and had a circus all to himself until he was lassoed and tied in a corner of the car with log chains. Oh, yes, they ship lots of mirrors, but the men don't like 'em. Seven years' bad luck to smash a looking-glass, you know. Snakes till you can't rest, but they keep them in boxes. Messengers don't mind 'em. Now you might think eggs are a nice freight, but they ain't. More expressmen grow bald on account of worrying over baskets of eggs than anything I know of," and Mr. Masters turned from the reporter to receive a package of hymn books consigned to a missionary among the Black Hills.

Before his death he gave information most clearly criminating Delano, the white leader of the band, who was in jail, and certain white confederates of his, persons who on account their wealth had heretofore defied justice. The negro stated that the wife of one of them had offered him $500. to burn the town. Yet in the face of all this Delano was not only not lynched, not only not brought to prompt trial, but was actually admitted to bail in the sum of $2000. on his promise to leave the country. We copy the just comments from the Houston Post:
The unexpected clemency of the people in reference to Delano, a notorious criminal, excites surprise and severe comment. Negroes who surrendered were shot down, but the ring-leader of the band, for some unexplained reason, is permitted to give bond and to leave the country. It is true we are not exactly in a position to judge of the policy of this extraordinary action of the Orange people. It is probable that they have adopted this method of getting rid of a bad character with his family and accomplices as the most obvious and easy of execution. But, in doing so, it should be borne in mind that they have left themselves under a reproach of compounding felony and something even worse, immediately upon the heels of a passionate breach of the law in the summary execution of Saxon and his companion. This is unfortunate in the last degree. The exigency of the occasion, the turbulence and excitement of the people may possibly be plead in extenuation for the precipitate action in reference to the killing of the negroes, though they cannot justify the violence. But the deliberate interference with the procedure of justice in the case of Delano, who should have been indicted for larceny, arson and murder, and his being turned loose upon the general community with the accusation of these crimes accompanying him wherever he goes, is an act not only indefensible but monstrous. We do not see how the people of Orange can defend their action in the premises. To be sure, they may thereby make a short-cut to the peace and order they so much desire, but the method by which this desirable end is obtained is both an illegal and an unmanly one. Why should they discriminate between Saxon, the tool, and Delano, the instigator? Why should Orange rid herself of a criminal citizen at the expense of the people at large?

A STRIKE IN SAVANNAH.
Riotous Conduct of Negro Laborers-A Police Sergeant Mortally Wounded Bloody Work Feared To-Day.
Riotous Conduct of Negro Laborers. A Police Sergeant Mortally Wounded—Bloody Work Feared To-Day.

SAVANNAH, September 19.—This afternoon the hands loading the New York steamer at the Central Railroad wharf without warning stopped work, and immediately interviewed the dramshops in the vicinity. At 3 o'clock they assembled in large force at the canal bridge leading to the wharves and obstructed the passage of drays and trucks, swearing that no work should be permitted on the wharves until their demand for two dollars per day, an advance of fifty cents, was allowed. The police barracks was telephoned and Sergt. H. H. Harvey, with two policemen, mounted, proceeded to the place. Sergt. Harvey rode upon the bridge and ordered the crowd to disperse, and there was a disposition on the part of the men to obey, but the violent and incendiary conduct of the women who encouraged them to resistance induced them to stand. The sergeant then rode into the crowd, when a negro woman dealt him a fearful blow with a large stick on the leg. He jumped from his horse to grab her, when some one in the crowd fired upon him, striking him in the breast an inch below the heart, inflicting what is thought a mortal wound, his condition to-night being considered hopeless. After being shot Harvey fired two shots into the crowd and it is thought wounded some one. The other policemen opened fire and the ringleaders dispersed.

Meanwhile a detail of twenty policemen, armed with muskets, double-quicked to the scene and the negroes abandoned their position and fled to the swamps. Large crowds, however, principally negro women, remained in the vicinity and were very defiant. The police remained at the bridge until dark, when the situation became quiet and they retired.

To-night a full force is out and the city is under guard. Meetings of the negroes were held, and it is rumored an attempt will be made to stop work on all vessels at 7 o'clock to-morrow morning. The authorities have been advised and arrangements made accordingly, and if any interference is attempted there will be bloody work. There is intense excitement in certain negro localities, and the streets are filled with drunken men. The steainship agents refuse to accede to the demand and telegrams have been sent to the country for negroes who are expected by the early train to-morrow. There are apprehensions of serious trouble.

A Fatal Accident.

This morning Samuel Davis, colored, aged 10 years, while fooling with an old musket accidentally discharged it, the contents lodging in the head of his sister Priscilla, aged 7 years, killing her instantly. This occurred on the Ogeechee road, eleven miles from the city.

In consequence of the excited feeling existing in the community and the ugly aspect of affairs, the Mayor, who had determined to preserve the peace of the city and put down, in the most summary manner, any general disturbance, about nine o'clock requested the commanders of the Savannah Volunteer Guards to have the members of their battalion assemble at the arsenal and be in readiness for any call that might be made upon them to assist the police. The Chatham Artillery were also summoned to their armory and to have two guns in readiness to be brought into action without delay. They were provided with canister, and it was distinctly understood and made known that in the event their services were called into requisition there would be work, as no blank cartridges were issued.

One thousand rounds of ball cartridges were also procured and deposited at one of the armories, where they could be easily procured and issued.

The Chathams were at their armory from one o'clock until nightfall, and the Guards, to the number of over eighty men, assembled at their arsenal at five o'clock in the afternoon and remained on duty until eight o'clock, when a detail was left in charge and a signal agreed upon which would call them together in a short time. The Georgia Hussars were also notified to be in readiness, and would have turned out fifty men.

It was decided only to use the military in case of grave emergency, and to assist the police force should they be found unable to quell any riot that might occur. These precautions were well taken, and the moral effect was good. The negroes who were thus threatening the peace of the city were by this movement put on notice that should they carry their riotous demonstrations too far that there would be no tampering with them, and that any riot would be speedily and summarily nipped in the bud. We are glad the occasion did not arise for calling into use the military, and the day passed off without serious disturbance. The arrangements that were made would have enabled the authorities to have suppressed any riotous proceedings.

ON THE WHARVES.

Whilst the centre of the excitement was in the vicinity of the Central Railroad bridge, there was a disquieting feeling all along the river front, and some timid draymen for certain business houses were afraid to go to the steamers to get freight. We heard of one case where a merchant was exceedingly anxious to obtain some goods without delay, but was unable to do so, as his colored drayman said he was afraid of being hurt by the discontented laborers. This was an exceptional case, though there were other firms that were inconvenienced by the delay in obtaining their goods. At the Baltimore wharf the hands under Messrs. Dixon Bros., who had been engaged unloading the steamship Saragossa, which was appointed to sail at four o'clock, resolutely refused to resume work unless their demand for an increase of wages was acceded to. As it was necessary, on account of some through freight to Europe, that the steamer should leave at the time appointed, the agents, Messrs. James B. West & Co., consented to pay the increase, but this concession is no index of their future action.

The Philadelphia and Boston steamers were subjected to like inconvenience, but the emergency not being so great with them the demands of the strikers were not granted. The steamship Gate City, which was taking on her freight when the strike commenced, was also appointed to sail in the afternoon. Her crew were brought into requisition and she finished loading and sailed on schedule time. The City of Macon came in yesterday, but in consequence of the interruption of work her cargo was not touched. She will be unloaded to-day, as arrangements have been perfected for securing sufficient force.

There was no interference with work at any of the presses or on any of the ships in the port, and with the exception of the wharves noted there was no visible excitement.

THE SITUATION SERENE.

Towards dark the crowds of negroes who had gathered in various parts of the city, and particularly the large crowd at the railroad bridge, among which were hundreds of negro women, who as usual were blatant and violent, began to slowly disperse. Many of these negroes, we understand, live five and six miles out on the road, and have been in the habit of coming into the city every day to work. They are more inclined to rioting than those who live in the city, but after a disturbance commences are the first to levant. After dark there were no persons in the neighborhood, though Fahm and Indian streets were filled, dotted with groups of men and women discussing the situation.

TO-DAY.

There was some apprehension expressed last night that the troubles would be increased to-day, but this belief is not general, as the preparations that have been made for the preservation of order will undoubtedly have a salutary effect upon the riotously inclined. We trust such may be the case, and the community relieved of the excitement and turmoil which have disturbed all classes for the past two days.

EFFORTS TO EFFECT AN ADJUSTMENT.

The serious aspect of affairs, and the certainty that a continuance of riotous demonstrations could have but one result, induced Lieutenant Colonel Woodhouse, Major Deveaux and Adjutant Toomer, of the colored battalion, three well known representative colored men, at the suggestion of some citizens, to go among the strikers and endeavor to check the spirit of insubordination and disorder which was so manifest. They made very conservative speeches, and advised the men, for their own sakes, to refrain from any acts of violence, and to take the peaceable method of petition for the adjustment of their troubles. The men listened with attention, and showed a disposition to act on the advice given, and it was decided to ask a committee of citizens to confer with Col. Wadley and ascertain what arrangements could be made. Captain John Flannery, Colonel J. H. Estill and L. H. DeMontmollin, Esq., consented to act as mediators, and at once proceeded to the railroad wharf, where they had an interview with Col. Wadley, who, after hearing the proposition of the strikers, replied that he was perfectly willing for the men to return to work at once, and then after this affair had quieted down, if they had any petition to make he would give it consideration, but under no circumstances would he make any promises as to his future course. Meanwhile a communication had been addressed by the Chairman of the strikers to a number of prominent Bay street merchants, requesting them to intercede with the employers with the view of effecting a satisfactory adjustment of the difficulty, which they agreed to do.

In the afternoon at 5 o'clock, an immense mass meeting of colored men was held at the foot of Bryan street, which was addressed by the colored officers above mentioned in the same style as in the morning, and afterwards by Mr. DeMontmollin, who stated the result of the interview with Colonel Wadley. The men seemed inclined favorably to take the course suggested—return to work at the old rates, and petition for an increase in a proper manner, but, after some discussion, it was decided to wait until 12 o'clock this morning to ascertain what had been accomplished by the other committee. The indications are that the negotiations will be successful, and that the troubles will be ended to-day, as the laborers will perceive that the only possible way to succeed in securing an advance in their wages is to adopt the course referred to, return quietly to their work and then make a respectful presentation of their claims for an increase. The more sensible among them are awakening to this fact, and as stated, there is good reason to anticipate an adjustment to-day.

PEACE MUST BE PRESERVED.

The proclamations of the Governor of the State and the Mayor of the city, which will be found elsewhere, will, we believe, have the effect of preventing any further disorder, and the excitement which has so seriously affected business the past three days will be allayed. The strong arm of the law will be exerted to preserve the peace and maintain order, and the turbulently inclined will find that they consult their own interest by realizing this fact.

Needed Improvements.

As has been before intimated in these columns, and as is well known to the better element in the community, Burrillville is in need of improvements in various directions. Improvement implies reform, and just how it is to be effected under the present unfavorable conditions is a conundrum which is difficult of solution. With a Town Council who utterly fail to appreciate the simplest needs of the people, and who fail, whether from lack of ability or for political reasons is not known, probably a combination of both, to enforce existing laws, or pass ordinances which have a tendency to prevent indecent exhibitions of the rowdyism elements in the town, it is perhaps, idle to expect any reform or improvement, but it would certainly be more agreeable to all peaceable citizens, and better for the reputation of Burrillville if our "executive department" could devise some way in which they can insure their re-election, and at the same time prevent the open and shameless disregard of all law; see that the amount appropriated for highways is expended in a sensible manner, even though thoroughness is impossible, and from the experience of other towns put some better interpretation upon the liquor law than at present, namely, "that all saloons within 400 feet of a school-house shall not pay a license." Perhaps that is not exactly the way the Council worded their interpretation of the law, but that is practically their verdict. And further, why is it that there is no attempt to enforce the law against the desecration of the Sabbath? Or, in fact, any other law, unless it happens that some citizen, from personal motives, causes the arrest and punishment of a violater of the statutes. Now, the plea of the Council is, so far as we have heard it, that they have appointed officers to enforce town and State ordinances, and can do no more. This is a foolish plea, and no one can blame an officer for neglecting to arrest guilty parties when he knows it will not be pleasant to the powers that made him an officer, and that the only result would be that he would secure an enemy and probably be deprived of his office, from which he may perhaps be deriving some income. The question is, who is to blame for the present disgraceful condition of things? It is the people who have put men into power who do not believe in correcting these abuses. There is no doubt that a majority of the voters could, if they would attend to their duties as citizens, and use their influence in favor of needed reforms, revolutionize this misgoverned town, and put men into office who have some weightier interest in the public good than is

SERGEANT HARVEY DEAD.
The Work of a Lawless Assassin Brought to a Close Yesterday Morning—The Funeral Ceremonies to Take Place To-Day—Measures Proposed for the Relief of His Family.
At five o'clock yesterday morning Sergeant H. H. Harvey, of the Savannah police, who was shot during the labor riots, which were inaugurated on the 19th of September last by the negro laborers employed on the Central Railroad wharf, died after a lingering period of suffering of one month. Everything which the affection of his family, the earnest regard of his many friends and the unceasing attention of his watchful and skillful physicians—Drs. Read and McFarland—could do was done to save a valuable life, endangered in the active and fearless discharge of duty, but all in vain. Yesterday morning his soul passed away into the presence of its Maker, and to-day all that is mortal of one of the truest men which Savannah has ever been able to count upon, either as a citizen or as a defender of her laws, will be consigned to the dust.

Sergeant Harvey was born in Bryan county on the 24th day of November, 1850, and was therefore, at the time of his decease, nearly thirty-one years of age. He came to this city in 1871, and on the 16th day of August of that year was appointed a member of the Savannah police force. Almost from the very day of his joining the force he showed himself to be honest in the extreme, fearless in any danger which he was called upon to confront, active in the discharge of every duty, and in all respects thoroughly reliable. Many were the notable instances in which these characteristics were displayed, and in this connection we may mention one which is still vivid in the minds of our citizens.

It will be remembered that on the 31st of May, 1876, Mr. Alexander Irving, when returning from an excursion of the Knights of Pythias with his little son, lost his footing and fell from the boat into the river. Mr. Harvey, who was on the boat at the time, saw him fall over and, without hesitation, and impelled solely by a desire to save a fellow man from death, plunged in after him. Owing to the darkness, his effort was unsuccessful, and both Mr. Irving and his child perished. The Knights, however, recognized the unselfish bravery of the noble deed, and, in token of their appreciation thereof, presented Mr. Harvey with a gold medal, which his widow still has and prizes most highly. We merely record this incident as illustrative of the true character of the gallant officer and brave soul, whose very bravery and gallantry led to his untimely end.

During his long and painful illness Sergeant Harvey bore himself unmurmuringly and with unfinching fortitude. To the last he retained all his faculties and would converse coolly and sensibly with friends about his bedside regarding his approaching end. Never was there a more striking instance of one being perfectly reconciled to leave the world. Convinced that his life had been square and true, and marked with fidelity to all trusts, he did not in the least dread to meet the grim messenger. To the contrary, as the last solemn moment approahed, feeling that earthly friends were powerless to aid him longer, he unhesitatingly put his whole trust in God, and knowing that his faith was well founded, and both feared no danger. Calmly and serenely he awaited the time in patience when he should receive the welcome summons "Well done good and faithful servant; enter thou into the joy of thy Lord."

After his decease, Coroner Sheftall having received due notification, proceeded to where his body lay and held an inquest over the remains. Doctors Read and McFarland and Messrs. John S. Higgins and James G. Bennett were all examined under oath, and gave in testimony establishing the facts already detailed as to the cause of his death. The jury have not yet rendered a verdict, having adjourned until four o'clock to-day to further consider the evidence. Doctors Read, Charlton, McFarland, Duncan, Myers, Sanders and Stone made an autopsy in hopes of discovering the ball which had produced the blood poisoning which caused the wound to result fatally, but it could not be found. It was a very small bullet, and, in the opinion of the physicians, had become imbedded somewhere in the spinal column.

Sergeant Harvey leaves a wife and one child, who are in straitened circumstances. It is the universal opinion, as far as we have heard it expressed, that the citizens of Savannah owe it to him who gave his life in their defense that these should be provided for. To this end several of his friends yesterday held a meeting, and, after the consideration, concluded to request the following named gentlemen to meet at Armory Hall to-day at 12 o'clock, to decide upon the best means for carrying out the object proposed: Messrs. S. P. Hamilton, R. H. Anderson, R. R. Richards, Thomas Ballantyne, Joseph A. Roberts, Felix Prendergast, Jacob Paulsen, Jacob Einstein, B. H. Levy, Daniel O'Connor, E. L. Neldlinger, E. Moran, W. B. Mell, W. G. Waller, D. B. Lester, J. L. Warren, R. N. Reed, James E. Walters, F. M. Hull, R. McIntyre, P. M. Russell, Sr., S. B. Adams, P. H. Ward, Jordan F. Brooks, J. J. Dale, Osceola Butler, John Flannery, S. Guckenheimer, Marmaduke Hamilton, P. W. Meldrim, E. A. Well, W. W. Gordon, H. M. Comer, George A. Hudson, R. H. Lewis, W. H. Turner, W. M. Sneed and J. Stern.

We feel assured that it will only be necessary to mention the subject to insure a hearty and generous response. The people of Savannah owe it to themselves to see that the wife and child of the man who fell a martyr to his duty, while protecting their lives and property, should be raised above all possibility of want.

The funeral will take place this afternoon at three o'clock, at Trinity Methodist Church, St. James square. The Masonic fraternity, of which he was a practical and zealous member, the Knights of Pythias and a detachment of police will attend, and we doubt not a large number of our citizens will avail themselves of this opportunity to pay their tribute to a brave, guileless, true man, and show their appreciation of his fidelity and worth.

SERGEANT HARVEY'S WIDOW.
Action Taken Yesterday to Save Herself and Child from Want-The Young Men's Historical Society and the John T. Ford Dramatic Association to the Front.
In accordance with the request of certain friends of the late Sergeant Harvey, as announced in these columns yesterday morning, a meeting of citizens was held at Armory Hall at 12:30 p.m. yesterday to devise ways and means for raising a fund to save the widow and child of the gallant deceased from present want and to provide for their future necessities. On motion Mr. S. P. Hamilton was unanimously elected Chairman of the meeting and Mr. Samuel B. Adams Secretary.

On being called to order the Chairman stated briefly the objects of the meeting, and Mr. P. M. Russell, Sr., made a motion that a committee of five be appointed to decide upon such matters as would be appropriate for the consideration of the meeting. This motion was unanimously adopted, and in accordance therewith the Chair appointed the following gentlemen as such committee: Messrs. P. M. Russell, Sr., Chairman; Thos. Ballantyne, S. Guckenheimer, D. B. Lester and D. O'Connor.

The committee then retired, and after due deliberation reported that it had been agreed to assign certain portions of the city to different committees to be canvassed for subscriptions, as follows:

Bay Street—F. M. Hull, Thos. Ballantyne, H. M. Comer, John Flannery, W. W. Gordon.

Savannah, Florida and Western Railway—Gen. R. H. Anderson, Felix Prendergast.

Bryan Street—E. L. Neidlinger, M. J. Doyle.

Congress Street—W. B. Mell, B. H. Levy.

Broughton Street—E. A. Well, John Lyons.

Public and Attorneys' Offices—S. B. Adams, P. M. Russell, J. J. McGowan.

River Street and all west of Jefferson—Daniel O'Connor, Jacob Paulsen.

Barnard to Bull, south of Bay—D. B. Lester, W. G. Waller.

Drayton, east and south of Bay—E. Moran, M. Lavin, John Schwarz.

South of Hall—John Sullivan, J. R. Hamlet.

Special Committee for Banks—S. P. Hamilton, S. Guckenhelmer.
Central Railroad—Edw. McIntire, B. J. Cubbedge, D. D. Arden, R. Barthelmess.
The committee also proposed that subscription lists be left at the various newspaper offices in the city, so that any person desiring to contribute might have the opportunity to leave their names at such offices, together with the amount of their subscriptions. This report was adopted without a dissenting voice.
A motion, offered by Mr. Neidlinger, that the secretary make out lists of the various committees, stating the territory assigned to them, and furnish the same to the chairmen of such committees, was adopted, as was also a motion offered by Mr. S. B. Adams, to the effect that whatever sums are collected be turned over to Mr. S. P. Hamilton as treasurer, and that when the collections were all in, that gentleman, as chairman, be authorized to reconvene the meeting for the purpose of deciding how the fund shall be invested for the benefit of Mrs. Harvey. In the meantime, however, he is to use his discretion in sending to her whatever sums he might ascertain to be required by her to meet her present necessities. He, as chairman, was also authorized to fill any vacancies in the existing committees which might accrue from any member being unable to serve, or from any other cause.
There being no further business to be considered at this time, on motion of Mr. Ballantyne, the meeting then adjourned subject to the call of the chairman.
The various committees enumerated above will begin to-day their work of canvassing. It is needless to commend their efforts to the generous consideration of our people of all classes. Sergeant Harvey met his death in the active and zealous discharge of his duties, and while gallantly exerting himself to protect the lives and property of our citizens. His widow and fatherless child have lost their mainstay and sole reliance for support, and are in need. We feel assured that it is merely enough to mention these facts to secure from the citizens of Savannah a hearty recognition of their duty in the premises, and a liberal response to the appeals which will be made to them for this most praiseworthy and charitable object.
Last evening the Young Men's Historical Association assembled at their hall, in response to a call from their President, Mr. S. S. Guckenheimer, to consider the subject of giving an entertainment for the benefit of the widow and child of the deceased. A good attendance was present, and, after Mr. Guckenheimer had stated the object of the meeting, a motion, made by Mr. P. Lewis, to the effect that an entertainment consisting of literary and humorous readings and a concert by the musical friends of the association, be given at the Theatre within two weeks, and on a date to be hereafter announced, was unanimously adopted. It was also agreed, without a single vote in the negative, that a committee of three members be appointed to take full charge of the entertainment, and that twelve citizens of Savannah be requested to act in co-operation with such committee; further, it was decided to place tickets for the entertainment in the hands of these gentlemen, and also in those of General R. H. Anderson and each member of the police force for sale. In obedience to this resolution the following committees were selected: Of the active members of the association—Messrs. H. G. Appel, J. Greenbaum and M. Gottlieb; of the citizens—Hon. John F. Wheaton, Chairman, Messrs. S. P. Hamilton, D. G. Purse, E. A. Well, Thomas Ballantyne, J. H. Estill, Daniel O'Connor, George C. Freeman, John Schwarz, Dr. William Duncan, J. A. Einstein and M. J. Doyle.

Besides this action of the Young Men's Historical Society, the John T. Ford Dramatic Association also held a meeting last evening, and decided to tender their services for an entertainment, to Mr. S. P. Hamilton, Chairman of the citizens' meeting. Messrs. M. F. Molina and George P. Gray were appointed a committee to arrange for such entertainment, should their offer be accepted, of which there is no doubt.

The prompt action of both these associations in this laudable cause are exceedingly commendable, and speaks well for the gentlemen composing them. We are confident their efforts will be highly appreciated, and that this appreciation will be substantially manifested by crowded houses at each entertainment.

OTTAWA, Oct. 20.—Referring to his Excellency's departure for England, it is semi-officially stated that there is no foundation whatever for the rumor that he will not return to Canada. His Excellency is only absent to leave, his full intention being to return early in January, and he will open the next session of Parliament, whenever that may be, in person. The Cabinet are understood to be considering the somewhat difficult question of appointing an Administrator of the Government to hold office during his absence. The practice has been during the temporary absence of the Governor-General from the capital, but within the Dominion, that a Deputy-Governor-General should be made to assume his functions for the time, as Chief-Justice Richle was during the recent Vice-Regal trip to the Northwest; but in the case of absence of the Governor-General beyond the bounds of the Dominion an Administrator is appointed. This duty has always hitherto been assigned to the commander of the forces at Halifax. SENATOBIA, Miss., September 11, 1881.
To the Editors of the Memphis Appeal.

On the night of the 9th instant, S. T. Eason, of Arkabutla, in Tate county, Mississippi, was murdered in the back room of his store. About 3 o'clock in the morning a noise was heard in that room by a mechanic who was employed by Messrs. Eason to build a room to the west side of their store, and who was sleeping in the unfinished room as the weather was warm. Fitner, the mechanic, went to the back window to see what was the matter, when some one pulled to the blinds. He then went to a neighboring store, waked the clerk and they returned to Eason's store, when some one got out of the back door, mounted a horse forty or fifty yards in the rear and ran off southward. Jeff D. Gillenwaters having been seen with the deceased late at night, and it having been supposed that he went to bed with him, was suspected, and his arrest was made in a few hours. A shirt was found covered with blood in the room and identified as Gillenwaters's; other signs pointed to him, in the shape of visiting cards of his, also sleeve buttons and studs. Pursuit of him developed traces of blood along his route, and when found his condition betokened the truth of former conjecture. He was after trial committed by the magistrate without bail. Excitement was high and many seemed willing to lynch him, but better and cooler counsels prevailed. Eason was a very popular young man, and his friends were greatly enraged. Gillenwaters is also of good connections, but, since this event, is said to have been somewhat off the line of good conduct which generally marked his family. He and his brothers were frequently about the store, always welcomed, and frequently slept there with Eason, between whom and there there was considerable friendship. Eason was found with his throat cut all around, terribly gashed, and his head badly contused by a sledge hammer lying near, or some heavy instrument. A razor was lying near with all the edge broken off and covered with blood by the cutting. It was a most shocking murder, and great indignation prevailed throughout this section. Memphis, Tenn., September 12.—Information has just reached this city of a horrible affair transpiring in the neighborhood of Senatobia, Mississippi, on Friday night. A young man named Gillenwaters was in jail at that plape supposed to be the assassin of a young merchant named Easton, of Arkabutia, Tate county, some time ago. Several other shots were fired into his prostrate body, when he was left for dead.
